title: Embeddings and Semantic Similarity
learning_outcomes: Explain embeddings and Semantic Similarity and connect at least two of its listed subtopics.
Apply the central idea in embeddings and Semantic Similarity to a small example or select a suitable approach for a stated scenario.
Identify an important assumption, failure mode, risk, or limitation and describe how it should be checked.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study embeddings and Semantic Similarity within Building Applications with Large Language Models. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: An AI application includes much more than a model call: data flow, validation, retrieval, access control, observability, and failure handling matter.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: An embedding maps an item into a numerical vector intended to preserve useful relationships for a task. Similarity scores depend on the embedding model, normalization, and evaluation data; they are not universal measures of meaning.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics covered in this lesson

items.title: What embeddings represent
items.text: An embedding maps an item such as a word, passage, image, or user into a vector. Similarity is meaningful only relative to the model, data, distance metric, and intended retrieval task.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Identify what embeddings and semantic similarity takes as input and what result or decision it is intended to support. 2. Read the example before running it and predict the output. 3. Run the small example, compare actual and expected output, then change one input or assumption and repeat. 4. Record what the example demonstrates and what it does not demonstrate about a real system.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with the task definition and the inputs available. Make the expected behavior explicit, choose a simple reference point, and inspect both ordinary examples and cases where assumptions may fail. An AI application includes much more than a model call: data flow, validation, retrieval, access control, observability, and failure handling matter.

content_blocks.code:
a = [1.0, 0.0]
b = [0.8, 0.2]
dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
na = sum(x * x for x in a) ** 0.5
nb = sum(y * y for y in b) ** 0.5
print("cosine similarity:", round(dot / (na * nb), 3))

content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original snippet or return to the small synthetic input, rerun it, and change one value at a time. Do not add real credentials, private user data, or untrusted code to the example.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: If the output differs, check indentation and spelling, confirm you saved the intended file, and compare each input value with the example. If the example runs as expected, do not infer that it proves a trained model works; this snippet is a deterministic teaching aid. Keep sensitive data out of tests.

content_blocks.title: Check before you trust a result
content_blocks.text: This is a small, deterministic teaching example—not a trained AI model or evidence of production performance. Run it with a local Python 3 interpreter; do not paste secrets or private data into experiments.

content.task: Try it yourself: sketch a small application for embeddings and semantic similarity with explicit inputs, outputs, and a failure path. Use a mock response rather than a live API key; validate output structure and test at least one unsupported or malformed case. The linked practice activity is: Semantic Search.

hints: Write down the inputs, expected output, and assumptions before changing the example.
Change only one input or condition and compare the results with your original prediction.
Ask whether the example covers realistic cases, important subgroups, and failure conditions; a toy example does not establish production reliability.
troubleshooting: Use Python 3 and run the file from the folder where it was saved.
If output differs, restore the original input and compare one changed value at a time.
If Python reports a syntax error, check copied quotation marks, indentation, and whether the full code block was copied.
